questions.prompt: Phosphorus (group V) is added to silicon. What kind of dopant is it, and what type of silicon results?
options: An acceptor; it makes p-type silicon
A donor; it makes p-type silicon because it leaves positive ions
Neither; group V atoms don't fit in the lattice
A donor; it makes n-type silicon (electrons are the majority carriers)
questions.explanation:
P's fifth valence electron isn't needed for bonding, so it is donated to the crystal as a free electron (reader Sec. 3.5.1). Free electrons outnumber holes, so the material is n-type.
The positive P⁺ ions are fixed in place and carry no current, so they don't make the material p-type. Acceptors (boron, group III) make p-type.

questions.prompt: Silicon is doped with \(N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) donors at 300 K (\(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)). What is the equilibrium hole concentration \(p_0\)? Scientific notation is fine.
questions.explanation:
Because \(N_D \gg n_i\), \(n_0 \approx N_D = 10^{16}\). By mass action:
\[p_0 = \frac{n_i^2}{N_D} = \frac{10^{20}}{10^{16}} = 10^{4}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\]
Holes are the minority carriers, outnumbered \(10^{12}\) to 1 (reader Eq. 3.36).

questions.prompt: Silicon is doped with boron at \(N_A = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Which carriers are the majority, and about how many are there?
options: Electrons, \(n_0 \approx 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)
Holes, \(p_0 \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)
Holes, \(p_0 \approx 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)
Electrons, \(n_0 \approx 10^{3}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)
questions.explanation:
Boron is an acceptor: each atom accepts a bonding electron and releases a free hole, so \(p_0 \approx N_A = 10^{17}\) (Eq. 3.37).
The electrons drop to \(n_0 = n_i^2/N_A = 10^{3}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\): they are the minority carriers.

questions.prompt: Very light doping: \(N_D = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), equal to \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). The approximation \(n_0 \approx N_D\) fails here. Use the exact charge-neutrality result \(n_0 = \frac{N_D + \sqrt{N_D^2 + 4n_i^2}}{2}\) to find \(n_0\). Scientific notation is fine.
questions.explanation:
\[n_0 = \frac{10^{10} + \sqrt{10^{20} + 4\times10^{20}}}{2} = 10^{10}\cdot\frac{1 + \sqrt5}{2} \approx 1.618\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\]
Not \(N_D + n_i = 2\times10^{10}\): the extra electrons speed up recombination, which also removes some of the thermally generated pairs. Check: \(p_0 = n_i^2/n_0 = 6.18\times10^{9}\), and \(n_0 - p_0 = 10^{10} = N_D\), so the sample is charge-neutral.

questions.prompt: A silicon sample contains both donors \(N_D = 3\times10^{16}\) and acceptors \(N_A = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) (compensation). What is the equilibrium hole concentration \(p_0\) at 300 K? (\(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\))
questions.explanation:
The acceptors soak up \(10^{16}\) of the donated electrons, so the material is n-type with \(n_0 \approx N_D - N_A = 2\times10^{16}\) (reader Eq. 3.39).
\[p_0 = \frac{n_i^2}{N_D - N_A} = \frac{10^{20}}{2\times10^{16}} = 5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\]
Common mistakes: using \(N_A\) as the hole density (the acceptors' holes recombined with donor electrons), or using \(N_D\) alone (gives \(10^4/3\)).

questions.prompt: Which equation states charge neutrality in a uniformly doped region (ionized donors \(N_D\), ionized acceptors \(N_A\))?
questions.explanation:
Count the charge signs: holes \(+q\), electrons \(-q\), ionized donors \(N_D^+\) are \(+q\) (they gave away an electron), ionized acceptors \(N_A^-\) are \(-q\). So \(\rho = q(p_0 - n_0 + N_D - N_A) = 0\) (reader Eq. 3.30, 5.18).
Combined with \(n_0p_0 = n_i^2\), this gives all the doping results. \(p_0n_0 = N_DN_A\) is a mash-up of mass action that isn't true.

questions.prompt: A silicon sample is doped with EQUAL concentrations of donors and acceptors, \(N_D = N_A = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). What are its equilibrium carrier concentrations?
options: \(n_0 = p_0 \approx n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\): fully compensated, it behaves like intrinsic silicon as far as carrier counts go
questions.explanation:
Neutrality: \(p_0 - n_0 + N_D - N_A = 0 \Rightarrow p_0 = n_0\). Mass action: \(n_0p_0 = n_i^2 \Rightarrow n_0 = p_0 = n_i\).
Gotcha: every donated electron fills an acceptor's empty bond, so the dopants cancel. The dopant IONS are still there, \(2\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) of them. They don't add carriers, but they do scatter carriers (lower mobility), so the sample isn't truly identical to pure silicon.

questions.prompt: Hot silicon: at about 600 K, \(n_i \approx 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). A sample doped with \(N_D = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) is at that temperature. What is the hole concentration \(p_0\)? (Careful about which approximation is valid.)
questions.explanation:
Here \(N_D\) is NOT much larger than \(n_i\), so \(n_0 \approx N_D\) is wrong. Use the exact result:
\[n_0 = \frac{N_D + \sqrt{N_D^2 + 4n_i^2}}{2} = 10^{15}\cdot\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2} = 1.618\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\]
\[p_0 = \frac{n_i^2}{n_0} = \frac{10^{30}}{1.618\times10^{15}} \approx 6.18\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\]
Gotcha: the naive \(p_0 = n_i^2/N_D = 10^{15}\) is off by 60%. At high temperature 'minority' holes are almost as plentiful as electrons, and the doping no longer controls the material. This is why chips have a maximum operating temperature.

questions.prompt: Adding donors to silicon LOWERS the hole concentration, even though donors never touch the holes directly. What is the mechanism?
options: Each donor ion captures a hole and neutralizes it
Donors turn holes into electrons
Holes are not affected; only the ratio n/p changes
The extra electrons raise the recombination rate (∝ np), while thermal generation stays the same, so holes are destroyed faster until np = nᵢ² again
questions.explanation:
\(G_{th}(T)\) depends only on temperature, but \(R = k\,n\,p\). More electrons mean a hole finds a partner sooner. The new balance needs a lower \(p\): \(p_0 = n_i^2/n_0\) (reader Sec. 3.5.4).
Gotcha: the fixed donor ions are positive and would REPEL holes; they don't bind them. 'Turning holes into electrons' doesn't conserve anything; recombination removes one of each.

questions.prompt: Preview of drift current: conductivity is \(\sigma = q(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)\). For silicon doped with \(N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) (\(\mu_n = 1200\), \(\mu_p = 450\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\)), what is the resistivity in Ω·cm?
questions.explanation:
\(n_0 \approx 10^{16}\), while \(p_0 = 10^{4}\) contributes \(10^{-12}\) as much, so ignore it:
\[\rho \approx \frac{1}{qN_D\mu_n} = \frac{1}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{16})(1200)} \approx 0.52\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\]
Compared with pure silicon (about 340 kΩ·cm), adding one dopant per 5 million atoms lowers \(\rho\) by about \(10^{6}\). That control of conductivity is what the drift skill builds on.

questions.prompt: Preview of carrier concentration versus potential: later you'll see that an n-type region sits at \(\varphi_n = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{n_0}{n_i}\) above intrinsic silicon. Find \(\varphi_n\) in mV for \(N_D = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) (\(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\), \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)).
questions.explanation:
\(n_0 \approx N_D = 10^{17}\) (doping fixes \(n_0\)), so
\[\varphi_n = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\times\ln(10^{7}) = 26 \times 16.12 \approx 419\ \mathrm{mV}\]
The '60 mV per decade' rule gives \(7 \times 60 = 420\) mV. A p-type region would come out NEGATIVE by the same amount. Put the two side by side and you get a built-in voltage: the PN junction.

questions.prompt: Preview of excess carriers: n-type silicon (\(N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)) is lit, generating an extra \(10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) electron–hole pairs. Which statement is right?
options: The electrons double, while the holes barely change
Both change by the same relative amount, a factor of 2
The minority holes rise from \(10^{4}\) to about \(10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), a huge relative change, while the majority electrons change by only 0.01%
Nothing changes, because \(np\) must stay equal to \(n_i^2\)
questions.explanation:
\(n = 10^{16} + 10^{12}\): up by 0.01%. \(p = 10^{4} + 10^{12} \approx 10^{12}\): up by a factor of \(10^{8}\).
Because the minority population starts so tiny, any disturbance is dominated by what happens to the MINORITY carriers. The excess-carrier and diode skills build on exactly this idea. (\(np = n_i^2\) only holds in equilibrium; under light \(np \gg n_i^2\).)
